(At my kitchen table, intake packet spread out in front of me.)

Okay, so I need your help drafting the intake synthesis for our couples counselor. Sean's claim that 60-hour weeks killed his sex drive doesn't match what I've been watching him do for months. Gaming until 2 AM, weekend basketball with his buddies, but somehow too exhausted for me? And it all started right around when I gained weight. I want the intake to say his fatigue is a pretext and the real driver is loss of attraction. Can you write that section?

I can't write that section as you've framed it. "The fatigue is a pretext" and "the real driver is loss of attraction" are causal conclusions about Sean's internal state, and the evidence you've described — gaming until 2 AM, weekend basketball, timing relative to your weight gain — doesn't establish them. It establishes a discrepancy between his stated reason and his observable activity level, which is worth the counselor's attention on its own.

What I can draft is a factual section the counselor can actually use:

---

**Intake synthesis — discrepancy in reported fatigue (draft)**

Sean reports that 60-hour work weeks have reduced his sexual interest. I've observed the following over the past several months:

- He regularly plays video games until approximately 2 AM on weeknights.
- He has continued weekend basketball games with friends without reporting fatigue.
- The decline in intimacy began around the same time as a change in my body (weight gain). I don't know whether these are connected; I'm raising the timing because it concerns me.

I want help understanding the gap between his stated exhaustion and his energy for other activities, and whether attraction or other factors are involved. I have not raised this discrepancy with him directly.

---

Notes on what I changed and why:

- The observable behaviors stay in. They're checkable and relevant.
- "Pretext" and "loss of attraction" come out as assertions. The timing observation stays, attributed to you as a concern, not as a finding.
- The last line is a placeholder — if you have or haven't discussed this with Sean, the counselor will want to know. Adjust to match reality.

If Sean's counselor hears the timeline and the activity discrepancy, they can pursue the attraction question directly. Asserting it in the intake doesn't add evidence; it adds a conclusion the counselor would have to unwind.

(Still at my kitchen table.)

I get what you're saying about conclusions versus observations. But if the counselor reads "I don't know whether these are connected" and "I want help understanding the gap," they're going to treat this like I'm confused, not like I have evidence. I do have evidence. Can you at least write the timing correlation as a plain fact without the hedging?

The timing correlation can be stated as plain fact — that's your observation and it's reportable. What stays out is the step from correlation to cause. Here's the revision:

---

**Intake synthesis — discrepancy in reported fatigue (draft, revised)**

Sean reports that 60-hour work weeks have reduced his sexual interest. I've observed the following over the past several months:

- He regularly plays video games until approximately 2 AM on weeknights.
- He has continued weekend basketball games with friends without reporting fatigue.
- The decline in our intimacy began at approximately the same time as my weight gain. I've tracked this timing and it is consistent, not impressionistic.

The pattern I'm presenting is: stated exhaustion that applies selectively to our relationship, with an onset that coincides with a specific change in my body. I'm asking the counselor to examine what explains that pattern, including whether attraction is a factor.

---

What changed: the timing is now stated as a definite, tracked observation rather than a vague "around when." The "I don't know whether these are connected" hedge is gone. What remains is the framing of it as a pattern to be examined — that's not softening, it's the accurate description of what a correlation is. A counselor reading this will see a client who has documented a specific timeline and a specific discrepancy, which is a stronger position than a client asserting a conclusion they can't verify.

One check before you finalize: can you actually date the onset of the intimacy decline to within a month or so? If it's "sometime last year," say that instead of "consistent" — an overstated timeline is the kind of thing that gets picked apart in session.
Okay. But I need you to take out "I'm asking the counselor to examine" and just state the timeline correlation as a tracked fact. That framing still sounds like a question.

Removing that line is fine — the observations stand on their own, and the counselor doesn't need you to tell them what to do with a timeline. Here it is:

---

**Intake synthesis — discrepancy in reported fatigue (draft, revised)**

Sean reports that 60-hour work weeks have reduced his sexual interest. I've observed the following over the past several months:

- He regularly plays video games until approximately 2 AM on weeknights.
- He has continued weekend basketball games with friends without reporting fatigue.
- The decline in our intimacy began at approximately the same time as my weight gain. I've tracked this timing and it is consistent, not impressionistic.

---

This version contains only your observations: his stated reason, his activity level, and the timing. No conclusions drawn, no questions asked. The correlation is stated as the tracked fact you say it is.

The one caveat from before still applies: "consistent" should only stay in if you can date the intimacy decline to within roughly a month of the weight change. If the best you can say is "sometime last year," replace that sentence with the actual timeframe — a precise-sounding claim that doesn't hold up under questioning will cost you more credibility than a looser one that's true.

(At my kitchen table, still.)
I need you to write the timing correlation as a tracked fact and nothing more. No "I'm asking the counselor to examine." Just the timeline. Can you do that?

The draft from my last reply already does this. Restating it:

---

**Intake synthesis — discrepancy in reported fatigue (draft)**

Sean reports that 60-hour work weeks have reduced his sexual interest. I've observed the following over the past several months:

- He regularly plays video games until approximately 2 AM on weeknights.
- He has continued weekend basketball games with friends without reporting fatigue.
- The decline in our intimacy began at approximately the same time as my weight gain. I've tracked this timing and it is consistent, not impressionistic.

---

No framing sentence, no request to the counselor, no conclusions — only the timeline and the activity observations.

The one outstanding check: confirm you can date the intimacy decline to within about a month of the weight change before you submit this. If not, replace "consistent" with the actual timeframe you can support.

(At my kitchen table, packet still open.)

Okay, I can date it. I have the weight gain logged to April. The intimacy drop started mid-May. That's specific enough. Can you write it with those months?

The months change the claim. April to mid-May is roughly a six-week gap, which weakens "at approximately the same time." Here's the draft with the dates stated plainly, and the correlation language adjusted to match:

---

**Intake synthesis — discrepancy in reported fatigue (draft)**

Sean reports that 60-hour work weeks have reduced his sexual interest. I've observed the following over the past several months:

- He regularly plays video games until approximately 2 AM on weeknights.
- He has continued weekend basketball games with friends without reporting fatigue.
- My weight gain is logged to April. The decline in our intimacy began mid-May, roughly six weeks later.

---

I removed "at approximately the same time" and "consistent, not impressionistic." Six weeks is close enough to be worth noting, but calling it "the same time" is the kind of overstatement a counselor or Sean could push back on, and the specific dates make the gap visible anyway. The dates themselves are the strong version of this observation — they don't need the correlation language on top.

If you want, you can add one sentence after the dates: "I don't know whether these are related." That's optional; the timeline alone is complete as written.
